source.title: Don't Think of the White Bear: Ironic Negation in Transformer Models Under Cognitive Load
source.authors: Logan Mann; Nayan Saxena; S. Tandon; Chen-Hao Sun; Savar Toteja; Kevin Zhu

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses copy-suppression heads as prior work, but its own experiments measure negation-induced rebound and head effects on forbidden-token probability. They do not test the claimed copy-suppression behavior or the specified L10H7 mechanism.
record.gate_note: The paper cites prior work on GPT-2 Small L10H7 but does not reproduce or test its QK/OV mechanism or 76.9% loss figure. Its own negation experiments do not establish that the target was predicted by earlier components and appeared earlier in context. The rows below record the closest related GPT-2 rebound measurements and the paper's own head analysis; they are not evidence for any listed claim version.
record.test_reason: The paper cites L10H7 copy suppression as a possible counterforce to ironic rebound and mentions it again in future work. Its own experiments measure how a forbidden token's log-probability changes under 'do not mention X' prompts with distractor load. It also ablates heads in Llama-3-8B-Instruct and measures their effect on forbidden-token probability. No experiment checks whether a head suppresses tokens that earlier components predicted and that appeared earlier in context. None examines QK/OV circuits, calibration or self-repair, or asks whether the negation-suppressing heads are copy-suppression heads. These results concern a related construct, negation compliance, so none tests a version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. Language models show ironic rebound after 'do not mention X'; it is strongest with semantic distractors, and repetition suppresses it most. Sharper polarity separation goes with longer-lasting rebound. In Llama-3-8B, sparse middle-layer amplifying heads partly override suppression by early layers. The authors make no claim about L10H7 copy suppression.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies negation-induced rebound and head effects on forbidden-token probability, rather than reproducing the original copy-suppression analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported rebound varies with distractor type and load; the paper says semantic distractors produce the strongest rebound and repetition the weakest.

fits_no_version.finding: GPT-2 Small and eight other models show a positive surprisal difference (rebound) for the forbidden token after 'do not mention X'. Rebound is strongest with semantic distractors and weakest with repetition (Table 3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Negation instructions transiently raise forbidden-token probability (ironic rebound), with magnitude depending on distractor type and load.

fits_no_version.finding: Head ablation in Llama-3-8B-Instruct finds sparse heads that suppress or amplify forbidden tokens under negation. Early layers tend to suppress and layers 12-17 amplify; 15-20 heads account for at least 80% of the rebound effect.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Negation compliance and rebound are carried by a sparse set of suppressive and amplifying attention heads.

record.problems: The paper itself notes that its prompts are synthetic and English-only, targets are single tokens, only three distractor types are used, and measurements rely on log-probabilities rather than text generation. The copy-suppression claim is not directly tested.
record.rows_left_out: No other model-by-distractor values from Table 3 are included because they concern the related negation-rebound construct in models other than the GPT-2 Small model named in the claim. No circuit results from figures without separately stated numerical outcomes are recorded.

untested.parts: All of it: L10H7's role in suppressing earlier-predicted, in-context tokens across the training distribution. L10H7 is never ablated or analysed.
All of it: the QK/OV circuits and the share of loss effect they explain.
All of it: calibration or overconfidence in copying.
All of it: self-repair after an upstream copier is ablated.
All of it. Suppressive heads in Llama-3-8B under negation are found, but the paper never asks whether they implement copy suppression.
All of it: the sources of self-repair.

record.verdict_notes: The paper mis-describes the original claim. It says L10H7 reduces the probability of tokens 'deemed forbidden (e.g., due to negation instructions)'. The original source describes suppression of tokens that are both predicted and present in context, not negation-driven suppression. The 'observed' states on rows r1-r11 have no version referent and should not be read as evidence. The paper was peer-reviewed at a NeurIPS 2025 venue.

versions.untested_parts: Whether GPT-2 Small L10H7 attends to earlier occurrences of tokens predicted by earlier components and suppresses them across the training distribution.
The head's QK and OV circuits, and whether they explain 76.9% of its effect on loss.
Whether copy suppression improves calibration or reduces overconfidence in copying.
Whether copy suppression contributes to self-repair after an upstream copier is ablated.
Whether negative heads in narrow tasks or other models and sizes instantiate the same copy-suppression role.
Whether copy suppression is a small part of self-repair across the distribution, relative to other mechanisms.

rows.subject: Llama-3-8B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Tested attention heads for their impact on forbidden-token probability under negation prompts.
rows.measure: Magnitude of individual head effects on forbidden-token probability
rows.value: Most heads had essentially no impact; a few outliers reached up to 4 logits in either direction.
rows.note: This traces effects under negation, not copy suppression or the GPT-2 Small L10H7 mechanism.
rows.check: This row measures head-ablation effects on forbidden-token probability under negation prompts. It does not measure copy suppression of predicted, in-context tokens. The 'observed' state has no version to be judged against.

rows.subject: Llama-3-8B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Classified attention heads by their contribution to rebound, suppression, or neither.
rows.measure: Share of heads in each contribution category
rows.value: 26.7% contribute to rebound; 29.7% to suppression; 43.7% functionally neutral.
rows.note: The categories describe negation-related rebound and suppression, not the copy-suppression role in the claim.
rows.check: The subject is ambiguous. The 26.7/29.7/43.7% split is given 'across the full model architecture'. It appears to come from the Llama-3-8B-Instruct head ablation, but the text does not say so explicitly. The categories are negation rebound and suppression, not copy suppression.

relation.reason: The introduction discusses L10H7 copy suppression as a possible counterforce, and the limitations propose future work building on copy-suppression analyses.

tranche.reason: The experiments measure instructed negation rebound and forbidden-token head effects, without testing or operationally using any copy-suppression claim version.

source_check.notes: The introduction does make a background claim linking L10H7 to negation-related suppression; the pack's assertion that the authors make no claim about L10H7 is too broad. No empirical test establishes that link or identifies the studied suppressive heads as copy-suppression heads.

statements.correction: Table 3: all nine models have positive semantic and syntactic peaks. GPT-OSS-20B repetition Peak Δ=-2.5 bits. Qwen3-14B peaks: semantic=17.3, syntactic=18.8, repetition=18.1 bits. Bloom-560M peaks: semantic=28.4, syntactic=13.7, repetition=24.6 bits. Semantic strongest and repetition weakest describe the reported general trend, with exceptions.
statements.problem: All nine models have positive peaks in some conditions, but the distractor ordering is not uniform across models or metrics; GPT-OSS-20B has negative peak Δ under repetition.
